content: Bitwarden's documented model (and a 2023 critique by palant.info of that exact design) sends a PBKDF2/Argon2id-derived Master Password Hash to the server, which the server re-hashes again (historically PBKDF2 100k iterations) before storing. Palant's critique: this server-side re-iteration adds negligible real security because an attacker who wants to brute-force the master password would derive the encryption key directly (paying the expensive client-side KDF cost per guess) rather than attack the low-value server-stored hash; the server-side slow-hash step mainly protects against the DB-leak case where the exact stored value alone must not be directly replayable as a bearer credential. Because this project's auth hash is HKDF-derived from an already-Argon2id-stretched master key (i.e. already high-entropy, 256-bit, not a guessable low-entropy secret), a fast cryptographic hash (SHA-256) is sufficient and correct for the server-side re-hash -- Argon2id-again server-side would burn CPU on every login for no additional resistance to offline guessing, since there is no low-entropy secret left to protect at that stage. A server-side per-user random salt for the re-hash (not reusing the KDF salt) is still worthwhile as defense-in-depth against precomputation/rainbow-table-style correlation across users.
